title: Glückel of Hameln, a Jewish merchant from Hamburg, wrote the memoirs of her life in Yiddish for her children

trailer.text: Glückel of Hameln, a Jewish merchant from Hamburg in the 17th century, wrote memoirs in Old Yiddish that are an invaluable source for Yiddish language and literature and for early modern Jewish history.
Glückel of Hameln was born in Hamburg to an affluent family of merchants, and with her husband Hayyim Hamel she was a successful Jewish merchant.
She was an active partner in the business, and after Hayyim's death in 1689 she continued to manage it on her own.
She wrote her memoirs in Old Yiddish to pass on to her children and their descendants the stories of the family's life.
The original manuscript was not preserved, but her son Moshe and her grandson Hayyim copied it.

The memoirs are considered an especially important social and historical document and one of the greatest achievements of Ashkenazi prose, in Yiddish or in Hebrew, at least until the end of the eighteenth century.

paragraphs.text: Glückel was born in Hamburg to an affluent family of merchants.
The family had commercial and familial ties to the court Jews and their surrounding circles.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, her father was the merchant Judah Leib, and her mother, Beila Melrich, was a businesswoman.
Her father saw to it that his children, sons and daughters alike, received an education.
According to JTA, she became knowledgeable in the Jewish musar tradition and in the politics of her day.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in 1649, when the Ashkenazi Jews ("the German Jews") were expelled from Hamburg, her parents moved to Altona.
According to the same source, after the Swedish invasion in 1657 they returned to Hamburg.
The sources disagree on the year of her birth.

stations.title: A young bride and business partner

paragraphs.text: At the age of twelve, Glückel was betrothed to Hayyim Hamel.
At the age of fourteen she married him and moved into his parents' home in Hamel.
Her husband's business was based mainly on trading in jewelry and precious stones.
According to the historian Rachel Greenblatt, the two newlywed teenagers grew the business from trade in second-hand gemstones to international money lending.
Glückel was an active partner.
She interviewed agents, considered potential partners, drew up partnership agreements and kept the books.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, she also helped with local pledges and contracts.
In her memoirs she wrote that her husband did nothing without her knowledge.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Glückel and Hayyim had 14 children, and 12 of them lived to marrying age.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, she carefully brought up six sons and six daughters and married them to members of the best Jewish families in Germany.
According to JTA, a plague struck Hamburg, and as the High Holy Days approached many Jewish families fled the city.
Glückel and Hayyim fled with their three young children, among them an eight-week-old baby girl.
In Hanover, the locals suspected that their four-year-old daughter, Tsipor, was infected.
The parents were forced to send her and her caregivers to another town, and were allowed to visit her only from a distance.
In her memoirs Glückel wrote that she leaves it to every good father and mother to judge for themselves how they felt.

stations.title: Alone at the head of the business

paragraphs.text: Hayyim lay on his deathbed and was asked whether he had any last instructions.
He answered that he had none, that his wife knew everything, and that she should continue as she had done until then.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, he died in 1689 from a fall.
Eight of her children were still unmarried and living at home, and Glückel continued to manage the family's business affairs in Hamburg on her own.
She also opened a sock factory in Hamburg, and took part in the trade fairs in other cities.

stations.title: A second marriage and a collapse

paragraphs.text: According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Glückel planned to move to the Land of Israel after marrying off all her children.
According to the same source, heavy losses in business changed her plan.
After eleven years as a widow she married the banker Cerf (Hertz) Levy of Metz, and moved to Metz.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, her second husband, Hirsch Levy, was a wealthy widower, a provisioner to the armies of Louis XIV and one of the leaders of the Jewish community in Metz.
Glikl wrote that she kept the betrothal secret to avoid the high tax she would have had to pay the Town Council for leaving the city for good.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, less than two years after the marriage Levy went bankrupt, and the couple lived in straitened circumstances.
According to World History Commons, he squandered the family's wealth.
In her memoirs, Glückel wrote that she fell into the hands of a husband and suffered the shame she had feared.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, when he died she was left penniless.
She spent her final years in Metz, dependent on her daughter and son-in-law and living in their home.
This was a situation she had always feared and had worked all her life to prevent.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the daughter was Esther and the son-in-law the banker Moses Schwabe, and she lived with them until her death in 1724.
Glückel wrote to pass on to her children and their descendants the life stories of their parents and family.
She wrote to them that she was recording this in case their children or grandchildren would not know who their family was.
According to the historian Rachel Greenblatt, she turned to the pen for comfort and self-therapy.
There are indications that she also wrote with other readers in mind.
She divided the book into seven chapters, which she called "books".
She wrote in Old Yiddish, rich in Hebrew elements and in numerous quotations from the Bible.
She did not have a good command of Hebrew itself, and once needed a Yiddish interpreter to understand a Hebrew text.
She drew on wide reading in printed Yiddish books: women's prayers, moral teachings, extracts from the Bible and story collections.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, she continued an established practice of self-description, by women and men, in ethical wills and personal narratives.
The Jewish Women's Archive describes her as a God-fearing, pious Jewish woman.
According to the same archive, the work abounds in descriptions of events in the Jewish community of Hamburg-Altona.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Glückel gave her writings their final form several years after the death of her second husband.
The work ends with an event from 1719, five years before her death, and it is not clear why.

stations.title: From manuscript to book and translations

paragraphs.text: The original manuscript was not preserved, but at least two copies were made: one by her son Moshe and one by her grandson Hayyim.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Moses Hameln, rabbi in Baiersdorf, copied the whole work from his mother's manuscript.
According to the same source, David Kaufmann edited the book from this copy, with an introduction, and it was published in Frankfurt in 1896.

In 1967 a 370-page Yiddish edition of the memoirs was published in Buenos Aires, published by the Yosef Lifshits Fund of the Literary Society at YIVO. Its record also lists Shmuel Rozhansky and Yosef Bernfeld.
The work is known mainly in translation.
Old Yiddish was no longer understood by the general public even in Kaufmann's time.
The first translation, into German, was made by a relative of Glückel's, Bertha Pappenheim.
The German translation by Alfred Feilchenfeld omitted her reflections, many of her introspective contemplations and most of the stories she wove into her writing.
According to Rachel Greenblatt, the earlier translations were incomplete or presented as biography and history.

The new English translation, Glikl: Memoirs 1691-1719, published by Brandeis University, is based on the 2006 Hebrew-Yiddish edition by Chava Turniansky, an Israel Prize winner and professor emerita at Hebrew University.
The translation includes her illustrations and meticulous notes.
Glückel's memoirs are considered a singularly important social and historical document.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, it is the first surviving extensive written document by a Jewish woman.
According to the same source, it is an invaluable source for Yiddish language and literature and for early modern Jewish history.
According to Rachel Greenblatt, these are rare memoirs from the period, and even rarer because they were written by a woman.
According to JTA, Glückel left a priceless window onto the lives of women, Jewish daily existence and religious observance in Germany.

According to World History Commons, her writings reveal the difficulty of being doubly marginalized: by the Christian community because of her religion, and by the patriarchal Jewish community because of her sex.
Only in the last two decades of the 20th century did the work and its author become the object of serious academic research.
According to Sylvia Fuks Fried, the memoirs have been explored from the perspective of Jewish history, of women's social history and of Glückel's role as a savvy businesswoman.
A conference marking the 350th anniversary of her birth was held in Hamburg, and its lectures were collected in a 2001 volume of articles.

claims.text: אף שגליקל הקדישה את דבריה לילדיה, יש סימנים לכך שכתבה גם מתוך מחשבה על קוראים אחרים.
claims.quote: Although she dedicates her words explicitly to her children, there are various indications that she was writing with an eye towards other readers as well.

claims.text: גליקל לא שלטה בעברית היטב, וכדוגמה היא נזקקה למתרגם ליידיש כדי להבין טקסט עברי.
claims.quote: thus, for example, Glückel requires a Yiddish interpreter to understand a Hebrew text

claims.text: גליקל שאבה מקריאה רחבה בספרי יידיש מודפסים, כמו תפילות לנשים, ספרי מוסר, קטעי מקרא ואוספי סיפורים.
claims.quote: She also drew upon her wide reading in Yiddish printed books, such as women's prayers, moral teachings, extracts from the Bible, and story collections

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה יודאיקה, גליקל המשיכה מסורת קיימת של תיאור עצמי, בידי נשים וגברים, בצוואות מוסר ובסיפורים אישיים.
claims.quote: However, Glikl was drawing from an established practice of self-description, by women as well as men, in ethical wills and personal narratives.

claims.text: ארכיון נשים יהודיות מתאר את גליקל כאישה יהודייה יראת שמים וחסידה.
claims.quote: a kind of manifesto of the faith, belief, aspirations, motives and opinions of this God-fearing pious Jewish woman

claims.text: לפי ארכיון נשים יהודיות, יצירת גליקל היא הרבה יותר מכרוניקה משפחתית, והיא מלאה בתיאורי אירועים בקהילה היהודית של המבורג-אלטונה.
claims.quote: Glückel’s work is far more than a family chronicle. It abounds in descriptions of events that occurred in the Jewish community of Hamburg-Altona

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה יודאיקה, גליקל נתנה לכתביה את צורתם הסופית כמה שנים אחרי מות בעלה השני.
claims.quote: gave her writings final form several years after the death of her second husband

claims.text: היצירה מסתיימת, ללא סיבה ברורה, באירוע מ-1719, חמש שנים לפני מות המחברת.
claims.quote: The work ends, for no apparent reason, with a reference to an event that took place in 1719, five years before the author’s death.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, בנה משה האמל, רב בבאיירסדורף, העתיק את כל היצירה מכתב ידה של אמו, ומההעתק הזה ערך דוד קאופמן את הספר.
claims.quote: Her son, Moses Hameln, rabbi of Baiersdorf and son-in-law of the court Jew Samson Baiersdorf, copied the whole work from his mother's manuscript, and from this copy David Kaufmann edited it.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, דוד קאופמן ערך את זיכרונות גליקל מהאמלן עם מבוא, והם יצאו בפרנקפורט ב-1896.
claims.quote: Die Memoiren der Glückel von Hameln, edited, with an introduction, by D. Kaufmann, Frankfort-on-the-Main, 1896;

claims.text: מהדורת יידיש של הזיכרונות יצאה ב-1967 בבואנוס איירס בהוצאת קרן יוסף ליפשיץ של אגודת הספרות שליד ייוו"א.
claims.quote: This edition was published in 1967 by Yosef Lifshits fond fun der liṭeraṭur-gezelshafṭ baym Yiṿo in Buenos Ayres.

claims.text: היצירה מוכרת בעיקר בתרגום, משום שהמקור לא הודפס מחדש ויידיש עתיקה כבר לא הייתה מובנת לציבור הרחב אפילו בזמן פרסומו בידי קאופמן.
claims.quote: Glückel’s work is known mainly in translation, since the original was never reprinted, and its language, Old Yiddish, was no longer understood by the general public

claims.text: התרגום הראשון, לגרמנית, נעשה בידי קרובת משפחה של גליקל, ברטה פפנהיים.
claims.quote: The first translation was rendered into German by a relative of Glückel’s, Bertha Pappenheim

claims.text: התרגום הגרמני המבואר של אלפרד פיילנפלד השמיט את הרהוריה של המחברת, רבים מהרהורי הנפש שלה ורוב הסיפורים ששזרה בכתיבתה.
claims.quote: but omitted the author’s reflections, along with many of her introspective contemplations and most of the stories she wove into her writing

claims.text: לפי רייצ'ל גרינבלט, התרגומים הקודמים היו חלקיים או הוצגו כביוגרפיה והיסטוריה, ולא היו נאמנים לטקסט המקורי.
claims.quote: But Greenblatt says those earlier versions were incomplete or presented as biography and history, and were not true to the original text.

claims.text: התרגום החדש כולל איורים והערות מדוקדקות של חוה טורניאנסקי, זוכת פרס ישראל, חוקרת ספרות יידיש ופרופסור אמריטה באוניברסיטה העברית.
claims.quote: with illustrations and meticulous notes by Israel Prize winner Chava Turniansky, a scholar of Yiddish literature and professor emerita at Hebrew University

claims.text: התרגום החדש מבוסס על המהדורה העברית-יידית של טורניאנסקי מ-2006, והמקור נכתב ביידיש עתיקה.
claims.quote: It is based on Turniansky’s 2006 Hebrew-Yiddish version of the memoir, which was originally written in Old Yiddish

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה יודאיקה, הטקסט של גליקל הוא המסמך הכתוב הנרחב הראשון ששרד מאישה יהודייה.
claims.quote: This carefully crafted text, interspersed with relevant folk tales, is the first surviving extensive written document by a Jewish woman.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה יודאיקה, האוטוביוגרפיה של גליקל היא מקור יקר ערך ללשון ולספרות היידיש ולהיסטוריה היהודית של העת החדשה המוקדמת.
claims.quote: is an invaluable source for Yiddish language and literature and for early modern Jewish history.

claims.text: לפי רייצ'ל גרינבלט, זיכרונותיה של גליקל הם זיכרונות נדירים מהתקופה, ונדירים עוד יותר משום שנכתבו בידי אישה.
claims.quote: Even rarer is that it was written by a woman, according to Rachel Greenblatt, a cultural historian specializing in the Jews of central and Eastern Europe

claims.text: לפי JTA, גליקל מהאמלן, אישה יהודייה מהמאה ה-17, השאירה חלון יקר ערך לחיי נשים, לחיי היום-יום היהודיים ולשמירת הדת בגרמניה.
claims.quote: one 17th-century Jewish woman, known as Gluckel of Hameln, left us a priceless window onto the lives of women, Jewish daily existence, and religious observance in Germany

claims.text: לפי ההערה באתר World History Commons, כתביה של גליקל חושפים את הקושי של היותה מודרת כפולה: על ידי הקהילה הנוצרית בגלל דתה ועל ידי הקהילה היהודית הפטריארכלית בגלל מינה.
claims.quote: Her writings reveal the difficulty of being doubly marginalized: by the majority Christian community because of her religion, and by her patriarchal Jewish community

claims.text: רק בשני העשורים האחרונים של המאה ה-20, עם התעניינות גוברת באוטוביוגרפיה והתפתחות לימודי המגדר, הפכו היצירה ומחברתה לנושא למחקר אקדמי רציני.
claims.quote: that the work itself as well as its author have become the object of serious academic research

claims.text: לפי סילביה פוקס פריד, הזיכרונות נחקרו בעבר מנקודת מבט של היסטוריה יהודית, היסטוריה חברתית של נשים ותפקידה של גליקל כאשת עסקים ממולחת.
claims.quote: In the past, the memoir has been explored from the perspective of Jewish history, women’s social history and Glikl’s extraordinary role as a savvy businesswoman, Fuks Fried said.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, גליקל נישאה לבנקאי העשיר צרף לוי ממץ ב-1700, בגיל חמישים וארבע.
claims.quote: at the age of fifty-four she married the wealthy banker Cerf Levy of Metz (1700).

claims.text: לפי ארכיון נשים יהודיות, התרגומים שנאמנים ברובם ליידיש המקורית כוללים את התרגום האנגלי של בת-ציון אברהמס.
claims.quote: The translations that are for the most part faithful to the original Yiddish include the following: the translation into English by Beth-Zion Abrahams

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה יודאיקה, כל התרגומים לזיכרונות גליקל, לגרמנית, צרפתית, עברית ואנגלית, משמיטים עד שני שלישים מהטקסט המקורי.
claims.quote: all of the translations of Glikl's memoirs, in German, French, Hebrew, and English omit as much as two-thirds of the actual text

claims.text: יידיש עתיקה כבר לא הייתה מובנת לציבור הרחב גם בזמנו של קאופמן.
claims.quote: its language, Old Yiddish, was no longer understood by the general public

claims.text: התרגום האנגלי החדש, "Glikl: Memoirs 1691-1719" בהוצאת אוניברסיטת ברנדייס, מבוסס על המהדורה העברית-יידית מ-2006 של חוה טורניאנסקי, זוכת פרס ישראל ופרופסור אמריטה באוניברסיטה העברית.
